items.stem: What is meant by an equinox?
items.answer: A day around 21 March or 23 September when day and night are of nearly equal length everywhere
items.markingKey: 1 mark: An equinox – a day around 21 March or 23 September when day and night are of nearly equal length everywhere.

items.stem: Imagine the Earth took 48 hours to rotate once but still went around the Sun in 365 days. How would day and night and the calendar change?
items.answer: Day and night would each last about 24 hours; there would be only about 182–183 such days in a year, so a calendar would have fewer, longer days; temperature differences between day and night would be larger.

items.stem: A lunar year is about 354 days and a solar year about 365 days. By how many days will a festival fixed by a purely lunar calendar shift in the solar calendar after 5 years?
items.answer: About 55 days earlier
items.markingKey: Each year the lunar calendar falls short by 365 − 354 = 11 days; 5 × 11 = 55 days.

items.stem:
Read: In a village, an elder says, "We sow wheat when the Krittika star group rises in the evening sky after the rains, and the harvest festival comes on the full moon of Vaisakh."
(i) Which kind of calendar uses star groups and the Moon like this? (ii) Why do stars rise at different times in different seasons? (iii) What is the phase of the Moon on Purnima? (iv) Why is such a calendar useful for farmers?
items.answer: (i) A traditional lunisolar calendar with nakshatras. (ii) As the Earth revolves around the Sun, the night side faces different parts of the sky. (iii) Full moon. (iv) It marks seasons reliably for sowing and harvesting.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem:
Read: A school calendar committee is planning holidays for 2031. Eid-ul-Fitr follows the lunar Hijri calendar, while Republic Day is always on 26 January (Gregorian, solar).
(i) Is 2031 a leap year? (ii) How many days does February 2031 have? (iii) If Eid falls on 16 March this year, about when will it fall next year? (iv) Why does Republic Day not shift like this?
items.answer: (i) No. (ii) 28. (iii) About 5 March (about 11 days earlier). (iv) It follows the solar calendar, which keeps pace with the Earth's revolution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Why do festivals like Eid come about 11 days earlier every year in the Gregorian calendar?
items.answer: They follow the lunar Hijri calendar, whose year (about 354 days) is about 11 days shorter than the solar year.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lunar calendar. 1 mark: 11-day difference.

items.stem: Why did ancient people build calendars based on both the Sun and the Moon?
items.answer: Lunar months are easy to count by watching phases, but seasons follow the Sun; combining both kept months easy to track while keeping festivals and farming in step with seasons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Moon easy to observe. 1 mark: seasons follow Sun. 1 mark: combination.

items.stem: A trekker is lost at night in a forest in Uttarakhand. Explain how she can use the Saptarishi to find the north.
items.answer: Find the Saptarishi (Big Dipper); extend the line joining its two pointer stars about five times their distance to reach the Pole Star; the direction of the Pole Star is north.

items.stem: A star is 4 light years away. When we see it tonight, are we seeing it as it is now? Explain what this tells us about looking at the night sky.
items.answer: No. The light left the star 4 years ago, so we see it as it was 4 years ago; looking at distant stars means looking into the past.

items.stem: Why would the Pole Star not be useful for finding direction for someone in Australia?

items.stem: Why does the Pole Star appear not to move while other stars do?
items.answer: It lies almost directly above the Earth's axis of rotation, so it stays in the same place as the Earth rotates.
